solutionSteps: \textnormal{Let the displayed upper degree bounds be denoted by the corresponding d symbols.}

\textnormal{Remove one exponential factor, then differentiate enough times to eliminate its polynomial. Weighted Rolle transfers a hypothetical excessive zero count to a space with one fewer exponential mode.}
\textnormal{Every remaining exponential rate is different, so differentiation preserves its polynomial degree. Induction bounds the zero count by the dimension minus one.}

\textnormal{To attain the bound, prescribe that many distinct real zeros. The corresponding homogeneous linear system has fewer equations than coefficients, so a nonzero function exists. The proved bound prevents further zeros or multiplicities.}

The real polynomials may have smaller degree or be zero, but f is not identically zero. What is the largest possible number of distinct real zeros of f?}

For sharpness, impose zeros at any dimension-minus-one distinct real points. There are fewer homogeneous linear equations than coefficients, so a nonzero coefficient vector exists. The zero bound and independence ensure a nonzero function with exactly those distinct zeros.

argument: The divisor sum counts positive lattice pairs with product at most n. Every such pair has at least one coordinate at most floor(sqrt(n)); count the two arms and subtract the square intersection.
Replace only the floor terms in each short arm by n/j; their total error is O(sqrt(n)). The harmonic expansion H_M=ln M+gamma+o(1), M/sqrt(n)->1, gives n ln n+(2gamma-1)n+o(n).
Each of the finitely many omitted terms floor(n/j)/n tends to1/j.

argument: For each fixed t the logarithms converge absolutely in the tail, hence the product is positive. Set L=ln(1/t) and J=floor((L/ln b)^(1/p)).

For k<=J the argument u=t*b^(k^p) is at most one, and ln(1-exp(-u))=ln u+O(u) uniformly. Since adjacent k^p differ by at least one, the sum of these errors is bounded by a geometric series independent of t.
For k>J, the first argument exceeds one and subsequent arguments grow at least geometrically. The tail sum of logarithms is uniformly bounded.
Thus ln P=-(J+1)L+ln b*sum(k^p)+O(1). The power sum equals J^(p+1)/(p+1)+O(J^p), and J=(L/ln b)^(1/p)+O(1). Dividing by L^(1+1/p) gives the stated constant.

argument: For each fixed t the logarithms converge absolutely in the tail, hence the product is positive. Set L=ln(1/t) and J=floor((L/ln b)^(1/p)).

For k<=J the argument u=t*b^(k^p) is at most one, and ln(1-exp(-u))=ln u+O(u) uniformly. Since adjacent k^p differ by at least one, the sum of these errors is bounded by a geometric series independent of t.
For k>J, the first argument exceeds one and subsequent arguments grow at least geometrically. The tail sum of logarithms is uniformly bounded.
Thus ln P=-(J+1)L+ln b*sum(k^p)+O(1). The power sum equals J^(p+1)/(p+1)+O(J^p), and J=(L/ln b)^(1/p)+O(1). Dividing by L^(1+1/p) gives the stated constant.

argument: Let y_j be cumulative sums and y_0=0. The denominator becomes sum(y_j-y_(j-1))^2. Its symmetric matrix has diagonal2 except its final entry1, and adjacent entries-1.
The sine eigenvector y_j=sin(j theta) obeys the left boundary automatically. The last row is equivalent to sin((N+1)theta)=sin(N theta), so theta_l=(2l-1)pi/(2N+1), l=1..N.
These N distinct eigenvalues are2-2cos(theta_l)>0. The smallest is4sin^2(pi/(4N+2)); reciprocal gives the maximum Rayleigh quotient.
With N=an+b, divide by n^2 and use sin u/u->1.

solutionSteps: \frac{\mathrm d^i}{\mathrm dx^i}=(g\prime)^i\frac{\mathrm d^i}{\mathrm dg^i}+\sum_{k<i}c_{ik}(x)\frac{\mathrm d^k}{\mathrm dg^k}

argument: Integrate the equation against each exponential Fourier mode twice by parts; periodic boundary terms vanish. The shift multiplies mode k by(-1)^k.

The coefficient factor is e^2-k^2 for even k and o^2-k^2 for odd k, so only the four signed frequencies survive. Fourier uniqueness for continuous periodic functions identifies the function with that finite trigonometric sum.

Orthogonality converts the given integral to the squared Euclidean coefficient norm. The derivative is a linear functional of the two sine coefficients, whose norm is sqrt(e^2+o^2). The displayed function attains it.
hypotheses: The real function is C2 and2pi-periodic. Its shifted second-order equation can be bootstrapped to all derivative orders.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The derivative has the same lowest nonzero Fourier frequency. It is orthogonal to every trigonometric polynomial of smaller degree.}

\textnormal{Suppose there were fewer than the claimed number of sign changes. Pair their cyclic locations and multiply the half-angle sine factors. The resulting trigonometric polynomial has smaller degree and can be given the same sign as the derivative everywhere.}
f\prime(x)T(x)\ge0\quad\textnormal{everywhere, and it is positive on an open interval}
\textnormal{Its integral is then positive, a contradiction. Sign changes are distinct derivative zeros. Finally the following admissible function attains the bound.}

argument: The derivative is orthogonal over a full period to every trigonometric polynomial of degree less than m.

If it had only2r sign changes with r<m, multiply the factors sin((x-x_j)/2) over its cyclic sign-change locations. With2r factors this is a real periodic trigonometric polynomial of degree r. A global sign makes its product with the derivative nonnegative and positive on an open interval.

The resulting integral is strictly positive, contradicting orthogonality. Hence at least2m distinct derivative zeros exist. The function cos(mx) is admissible and has exactly2m critical points in a half-open period.
hypotheses: The trigonometric polynomial is real and its first frequency pair is not both zero. Thus its derivative is a nonzero real trigonometric polynomial.

executedChecks.detail: At level j there are2^(j-1) summands, each with Lipschitz constant lambda^j.

argument: The function series converges uniformly on bounded intervals. Every difference quotient is bounded in absolute value by the summable level majorant2^(j-1)lambda^j. Since no corner equals the evaluation point, dominated convergence passes the derivative through the infinite sum.
At level j the derivative is lambda^j times the number of dyadic odd numerators to the left minus the number to the right. This count is2 floor((2^j a+1)/2)-2^(j-1).
Separate its linear2^j part from the bounded residue epsilon_j. The odd denominator makes the binary residue periodic, giving the two geometric sums displayed.
hypotheses: The evaluation point has odd denominator and is not dyadic. The ratio is strictly between zero and one half.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Test joint equidistribution with an arbitrary nonzero integer Fourier character.}
\textnormal{When the quadratic coefficient vanishes this is a geometric sum with nonunit ratio. Otherwise every fixed-lag correlation has the linear phase below.}

\textnormal{Its mean tends to zero because its slope is irrational. Van der Corput gives squared limsup at most one over an arbitrary window length; letting that length grow proves every nontrivial character has zero mean.}
\textnormal{Weyl criterion now applies jointly; arithmetic dependence has been checked rather than treated as independence.}

executedChecks.description: Quadratic phase differencing leaves a linear irrational coefficient
executedChecks.left: 2 \sqrt{2} N b h + \sqrt{2} a h + \sqrt{2} b h^{2}
executedChecks.right: 2 \sqrt{2} N b h + \sqrt{2} \left(a h + b h^{2}\right)

executedChecks.description: Independent triangle integration gives the limiting moment

argument: For a nonzero character(a,b), the exponential phase is square-root-two times(a*n+b*n squared). If b=0, the average is a geometric sum with ratio different from one and tends to zero.
If b is nonzero, every fixed positive-lag correlation has a linear phase with nonzero irrational slope2*b*h*sqrt2, so it also tends to zero by the same geometric-sum estimate.
The van der Corput inequality, with a fixed correlation window H and then the sample size tending to infinity, bounds the squared limsup of the original average by1/H. Let H tend to infinity.

Weyl criterion therefore gives joint uniformity on the square. The fractional-coordinate distance power is bounded and has discontinuities only on the boundary identifications, a null set, so Riemann-integrable equidistribution applies.
Split the square along the diagonal and integrate twice the lower triangle to obtain the exact moment.
hypotheses: The fixed irrational coefficient is square root two. Fourier character indices are integers, not both zero. The distance power is a positive integer.

solutionSteps: k_+=(1+\varepsilon)\frac{\ln n}{\ln\ln n},\qquad\Pr(M_n\ge\lceil k_+\rceil)\le\frac n{\lceil k_+\rceil!}\longrightarrow0
\textnormal{For the lower bound, temporarily make the box counts independent Poisson variables with mean one.}

Factorial-moment union-bound combinatorics

argument: For k=(1+epsilon)ln n/ln ln n, the binomial factorial-moment bound gives P(M_n>=k)<=n/k!; Stirling makes its logarithm at most minus epsilon ln n plus lower-order terms.
For the lower bound use independent Poisson-one counts Y_1,...,Y_n. For k=(1-epsilon)ln n/ln ln n, P(Y_i>=k)>=e^-1/k!=n^(-1+epsilon+o1), so P(max Y_i<k)<=exp(-n^(epsilon+o1)).

Conditioned on sum Y_i=n, the counts have exactly the original multinomial occupancy law. Stirling gives P(sum Y_i=n) asymptotic to1/sqrt(2pi n). Dividing the exponentially small failure probability by this conditioning probability still gives zero.
Combining upper and lower estimates for every fixed positive epsilon proves the stated convergence in probability. Floor and ceiling of the threshold affect only lower-order terms.
hypotheses: Exactly n independent balls choose uniformly among exactly n boxes. The maximum load is the number of balls in the fullest box.

argument: Lagrange inversion gives a_n=(1/n)[u^(n-1)]exp(n(u+cu squared)). Integrate on the circle u=tau exp(i theta).
After extracting rho^(-n), the remaining prefactor is tau/n and the integral is exp(n Phi(theta))exp(i theta), divided by2pi. Stationarity is tau+2c tau squared=1.
The real phase equals tau(cos theta-1)+c tau squared(cos2theta-1). Its unique maximum on[-pi,pi] is zero at theta0; outside every fixed neighborhood it is bounded above by a negative constant.

Near zero Phi(theta)=-variance*theta squared/2+O(theta cubed), with variance=tau+4c tau squared>0. Rescale theta=v/sqrt(n), dominate by a fixed Gaussian in a small neighborhood, and discard the exponentially small complement.
The local integral is asymptotic to sqrt(2pi/(n*variance)). Multiplying the coefficient prefactor gives tau/sqrt(2pi*variance), with the power n^(-3/2).
hypotheses: The positive quadratic exponential coefficient and critical point are the displayed finite rational values. The analytic implicit solution exists uniquely near zero by the implicit-function theorem.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{A cycle of length k on labelled elements contributes one over k to the exponential generating function. Taking an unordered collection of allowed cycles exponentiates their contributions.}
\textnormal{Let }q_N\textnormal{ be the analogous probability on N labels, so }p_n=q_{3n}.\qquad\sum_{N\ge0}q_Nz^N=\exp\left(\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{z^{3j}}{3j}\right)=(1-z^{3})^{-\frac{1}{3}}
\textnormal{The ambient factorial has already canceled because these are probabilities, not counts. Stirling at two fixed shifts gives the ratio below.}
statement: \textnormal{Choose a permutation uniformly from all permutations of }\{1,2,\ldots,3n\}.\textnormal{Let }p_n\textnormal{ be the probability that every cycle has length divisible by }3\textnormal{. With }\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm dt\quad(a>0),\textnormal{evaluate }\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{\frac{2}{3}}p_n.

argument: A labelled cycle of length k has(k-1)! arrangements, so its exponential generating contribution is z^k/k. Unordered collections of allowed cycles exponentiate their sum.
The probability generating series is exp(sum z^(dj)/(dj))=(1-z^d)^(-1/d). Therefore the desired probability is(1/d)_n/n!, with no extra factorial from the ambient size.
Write this coefficient as Gamma(n+1/d)/(Gamma(1/d)Gamma(n+1)). Stirling applied at the two shifted arguments gives the ratio n^(1/d-1)(1+o1).
The requested normalization uses n, not the total number d*n of labels.
hypotheses: The permutation is uniform on the full symmetric group of size d*n; all cycles, including singleton cycles, are subject to the divisibility condition.
The Gamma function is defined for positive arguments.

\textnormal{Let }q_N\textnormal{ be the analogous probability on N labels, so }p_n=q_{16n}.\qquad\sum_{N\ge0}q_Nz^N=\exp\left(\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{z^{16j}}{16j}\right)=(1-z^{16})^{-\frac{1}{16}}
\textnormal{The ambient factorial has already canceled because these are probabilities, not counts. Stirling at two fixed shifts gives the ratio below.}
statement: \textnormal{Choose a permutation uniformly from all permutations of }\{1,2,\ldots,16n\}.\textnormal{Let }p_n\textnormal{ be the probability that every cycle has length divisible by }16\textnormal{. With }\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm dt\quad(a>0),\textnormal{evaluate }\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{\frac{15}{16}}p_n.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The first factor is return to zero at the specified time. A reflection count gives the second factor as the probability of no later return, and independence supplies their product.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{All coefficient profiles are uniformly above the spectral edge. In particular, a common positive lower bound for every eigenvalue is }\delta=2\cosh1-2>0.

\textnormal{Cut the matrix into blocks of about square-root n rows and freeze the diagonal in each block. The removed links have total rank of order square-root n; the freezing error has operator norm of order inverse square-root n.}
\textnormal{The rank bound follows from uniform relative-eigenvalue bounds. The small-norm bound follows by integrating the trace formula for the derivative of a logarithmic determinant.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{All coefficient profiles are uniformly above the spectral edge. In particular, a common positive lower bound for every eigenvalue is }\delta=2\cosh1-2>0.

\textnormal{Cut the matrix into blocks of about square-root n rows and freeze the diagonal in each block. The removed links have total rank of order square-root n; the freezing error has operator norm of order inverse square-root n.}
\textnormal{The rank bound follows from uniform relative-eigenvalue bounds. The small-norm bound follows by integrating the trace formula for the derivative of a logarithmic determinant.}

\textnormal{For a constant block with diagonal }2\cosh u\textnormal{ and adjacent off-diagonal entries one, let }D_m\textnormal{ denote its determinant when its size is }m\textnormal{ by }m\textnormal{.}
statement: g(x)=11 x^{4} - 12 x^{3} + 4 x + 1.\textnormal{For each positive integer n, let A be the n by n real tridiagonal matrix with }A_{jj}=2\cosh(g(j/n))\ (1\le j\le n),\qquad A_{j,j+1}=A_{j+1,j}=1,\textnormal{and all other entries zero. Determine }\lim_{n\to\infty}(\det A)^{1/n}.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Above the largest diagonal entry, the determinant lemma gives the strictly decreasing secular equation.}

\textnormal{The selected coupling is above the edge threshold because the displayed integral is strictly smaller than its edge value. Thus the limiting equation has the unique root shown, separated from the edge.}

\textnormal{The finite sums converge at any two fixed points on opposite sides of that root. Their monotonicity traps the finite largest eigenvalue between those points. Shrinking the bracket proves convergence.}
statement: \lambda=\frac{1}{1 - \frac{\ln{\left(5 \right)}}{4}}.\textnormal{For positive integers n, define a real symmetric matrix }A_n=\operatorname{diag}(0,1/n,\ldots,(n-1)/n)+\frac\lambda n vv^{\mathsf T},\qquad v_j=(1-j/n)^{\frac{1}{2}}\ (0\le j<n).\textnormal{Find the limit of the largest eigenvalue of }A_n.

argument: The determinant lemma makes the unique eigenvalue above the largest diagonal entry solve1=(lambda/n)sum(1-j/n)^p/(rho-j/n). The right side is strictly decreasing from infinity to zero on that interval.
For any rho>1 the sum converges to I_p(rho)=integral0to1(1-t)^p/(rho-t)dt, locally uniformly away from1. At the edge its limiting value is1/p, while it strictly decreases to zero at infinity.

The specified lambda=1/I_p(r) exceeds p, so the limiting equation has the unique root r>1. Choose two fixed points just below and above r, still above1; strict monotonicity and Riemann convergence trap the finite roots between them for all large n.
As the two trapping points approach r, the largest eigenvalue converges to r. All remaining eigenvalues lie below this one by the monotone secular equation or rank-one interlacing.
hypotheses: The perturbation coupling is positive; the vector coordinates are positive because the diagonal grid stops before1.
The chosen rational target exceeds1, and the power is a positive integer.

argument: Factor the interval powers from rows and columns: the total power is n(n-1)+alpha n. The remaining Cauchy determinant is product(j!)^2 divided by product(i+j+alpha).
The numerator logarithm, divided by n^2, equals ln n plus the integral2 integral_0^1(1-u)ln u, up to o(1).

The denominator similarly equals ln n plus the unit-square integral ln(u+v), up to o(1). The logarithmic singularities are integrable; truncation near the endpoints and monotone integral bounds control them uniformly. The fixed positive shift alpha changes only an o(n^2) term.
Subtracting cancels ln n and leaves -2ln2. The interval factor adds ln(length), giving the asserted root limit.

argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.
hypotheses: The exclusion modulus is an integer at least two, so part one is always allowed. Part multiplicities are unrestricted nonnegative integers. The infinite product converges at every positive real t.

argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.
hypotheses: The exclusion modulus is an integer at least two, so part one is always allowed. Part multiplicities are unrestricted nonnegative integers. The infinite product converges at every positive real t.

argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.
hypotheses: The exclusion modulus is an integer at least two, so part one is always allowed. Part multiplicities are unrestricted nonnegative integers. The infinite product converges at every positive real t.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The endpoint singularity is integrable and the tail is exponentially bounded. The nonnegative logarithmic series evaluates the integral term by term. Removing the forbidden multiples gives}
\textnormal{The reverse bound needs coefficient information. Give each allowed part size an independent geometric multiplicity and let N be the resulting total size.}
\textnormal{These follow from separate Riemann sums for the first and second geometric moments, so no derivative of an asymptotic formula is assumed.}

\textnormal{Chebyshev applies because the variance is of order n to the three-halves power, smaller than the squared window width. Adding parts of size one injects every partition at a smaller size into the target size.}
\textnormal{Take logarithms, divide by the square root of n, and let epsilon tend to zero. The lower bound matches the upper bound.}

argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.
hypotheses: The exclusion modulus is an integer at least two, so part one is always allowed. Part multiplicities are unrestricted nonnegative integers. The infinite product converges at every positive real t.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The endpoint singularity is integrable and the tail is exponentially bounded. The nonnegative logarithmic series evaluates the integral term by term. Removing the forbidden multiples gives}
\textnormal{The reverse bound needs coefficient information. Give each allowed part size an independent geometric multiplicity and let N be the resulting total size.}
\textnormal{These follow from separate Riemann sums for the first and second geometric moments, so no derivative of an asymptotic formula is assumed.}

\textnormal{Chebyshev applies because the variance is of order n to the three-halves power, smaller than the squared window width. Adding parts of size one injects every partition at a smaller size into the target size.}
\textnormal{Take logarithms, divide by the square root of n, and let epsilon tend to zero. The lower bound matches the upper bound.}

argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.
hypotheses: The exclusion modulus is an integer at least two, so part one is always allowed. Part multiplicities are unrestricted nonnegative integers. The infinite product converges at every positive real t.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For the first identity use the increasing substitution below and evenness of the resulting whole-line integrand.}
\textnormal{For the second identity use the following decreasing substitution on the interval from zero to b. It maps onto the interval from A to infinity and contributes a factor one half.}
\textnormal{Arithmetic and geometric means converge to a common positive value, so the parameters tend to zero. For the complementary integral use its tangent-variable representation.}

\textnormal{Split the improper integral at one and at the inverse square root of m. The outer parts stay bounded. In the middle, subtract one over u; the error is bounded by a constant times the sum of inverse-cubic u and m times u, with bounded integral.}
\textnormal{To determine the requested prefactor, the bounded error in the logarithm is insufficient. Retain the exact endpoint constant using a symmetric cutoff.}

\textnormal{The inversion below preserves the integral and exchanges the two pieces at the cutoff. On the lower piece, replacing the second square root by one incurs an error of order the square root of m.}
\textnormal{The ordinary invariant also determines the positive common limit. Combine it with the exact coordinate-difference formula.}
statement: a_0=1,\quad b_0=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3},\qquad a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n+b_n}{2},\quad b_{n+1}=\sqrt{a_nb_n}.\textnormal{Use the parameter convention }K(p)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\sqrt{1-p\sin^2\theta}}\quad(0<p<1).q=e^{- \frac{\pi K\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)}{K\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}}.\textnormal{Find the normalized shrinking-gap limit }\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n-b_n}{q^{2^n}}.

argument: In the tangent representation of K(1-m), the inversion t=1/(sqrt(m)*u) leaves the integral kernel invariant. Split at its fixed point T=m^(-1/4), obtaining exactly twice the integral from0toT.
On this interval replace(1+m*t squared)^(-1/2) by1. The absolute integrated error is bounded by C*m*integral0T t squared/sqrt(1+t squared)dt=O(sqrt(m)).
The remaining integral is2asinh(T)=ln4-(1/2)ln m+O(sqrt(m)). Together with K(m)=pi/2+O(m), this gives exp(-pi*K(1-m)/K(m))=(m/16)(1+o1).

Complementary doubling makes this exponential exactly q^(2^n) at iteration n. Hence m_n is asymptotic to16q^(2^n). The coordinate difference equals a_n*m_n/(1+sqrt(1-m_n)), so its normalized limit is8M, where M=pi/(2K(p)).
hypotheses: The ordinary and complementary integral identities above hold on the positive branch. The parameter m tends to zero through positive values.

argument: Define I(a,b)=integral0infinity dt/sqrt((t^2+a^2)(t^2+b^2)) and J(a,b)=integral0b dt/sqrt((a^2-t^2)(b^2-t^2)). The substitutions t=b tan theta and t=b sin theta give I=K(m)/a and J=K(1-m)/a.
For I use u=(t-ab/t)/2. It is an increasing bijection onto the real line; the two factorizations and its Jacobian give I(a,b)=I((a+b)/2,sqrt(ab)), using evenness.

For J use u=(t+ab/t)/2 on0<t<b. This is decreasing from infinity to(a+b)/2; both square-root factors stay positive. It gives one half the integral from the arithmetic mean to infinity of[(u^2-A^2)(u^2-G^2)]^(-1/2). The inversion v=A*G/u converts that exterior integral exactly to J(A,G). Thus J(A,G)=2J(a,b).
Consequently R_n=K(1-m_n)/K(m_n) equals2^n R_0. The ordinary arithmetic/geometric inequalities show both coordinates tend to a common positive limit, so m_n tends to zero.

For small m, K(m)=pi/2+O(m). In K(1-m)=integral0infinity du/sqrt((1+u^2)(1+m u^2)), split at1 and1/sqrt(m). The first and last pieces are uniformly bounded. On the middle interval the difference from1/u is bounded by a constant times(u^-3+m*u), whose integral is uniformly bounded. Hence K(1-m)=-(1/2)ln m+O(1).
It follows that pi R_n=-ln m_n+O(1). Also a_n-b_n=a_n*m_n/(1+sqrt(1-m_n)), whose ratio to m_n stays between positive constants. Divide logarithms by2^n and exponentiate to get the stated nome.
hypotheses: At every step a>b>0. The elliptic parameter is m=1-(b/a)^2, strictly between zero and one. All square roots use the positive real branch.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{In the determinant expansion by column multilinearity, the quadratic coefficient selects two diagonal increments. Each selection leaves the principal minor obtained by deleting those two coordinates.}
\textnormal{A tridiagonal path block of length }k\textnormal{ with diagonal entries two and neighbor entries minus one has determinant }D_k\textnormal{.}
\textnormal{Deleting two cycle vertices at cyclic distance }r\textnormal{ leaves path lengths }r-1\textnormal{ and }4-r-1\textnormal{. Their determinant product is }r(4-r)\textnormal{.}
\textnormal{Each unordered pair was counted twice by starting vertex and cyclic distance. Finally convert the quadratic coefficient to a second derivative.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The fixed shift in the question is}
\textnormal{For every nonzero integer frequency, the orbit has a vanishing exponential average: the geometric-sum numerator stays bounded and its denominator is nonzero.}
\textnormal{Weyl’s criterion therefore makes the fractional parts uniformly distributed. Their correlated product is a Riemann-integrable function of the same orbit coordinate.}

analyticCertificate: For every nonzero integer h, exp(2pi i h sqrt(2)) differs from one. The finite geometric sum of its first N powers has bounded numerator, so its average tends to zero.

Weyl criterion therefore makes {k sqrt(2)} uniformly distributed on [0,1]. The function q(t)=t{t+a} is bounded and has only one discontinuity, hence is Riemann integrable and its orbit averages converge to its integral.
For 0<=t<1-a, q=t(t+a); for 1-a<=t<1, q=t(t+a-1). Integrating the two quadratics yields 1/3-a/2+a^2/2.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Subtract the line interpolating the two endpoint values of the polynomial.}
\textnormal{The numerator vanishes at both endpoints. Dividing by the simple sine zeros gives a continuously differentiable extension of this quotient.}
\textnormal{The remaining integral tends to zero by this integration-by-parts bound, leaving only the endpoint-line contribution.}

analyticCertificate: For every integer N>=0, sin((2N+1)x)/sin x=1+2 sum_(j=1)^N cos(2jx), with continuous endpoint values. Its integral on0..pi is pi.
The kernel is invariant under x->pi-x. For f=x^m, reflection shows the integral of its endpoint-interpolating line ell(x)=pi^(m-1)x equals pi^(m+1)/2.
The polynomial h=f-ell vanishes at both endpoints. Hence g=h/sin x extends to a continuously differentiable function on the closed interval.
The residual is integral g(x)sin((2N+1)x)dx. Integration by parts bounds it by (|g(0)|+|g(pi)|+integral|g prime|)/(2N+1), which tends to zero.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{These Chebyshev polynomials have leading coefficient given by the recurrence. Scaling produces a monic polynomial on the stated interval.}
\textnormal{The maximum absolute value of this polynomial is the displayed amplitude, attained with alternating signs at one more point than its degree.}

\textnormal{If a monic competitor had a smaller maximum, subtracting this polynomial would give alternating signs at those points. The difference would have at least as many distinct roots as the original degree, although its degree is smaller. This is impossible.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For a fixed number of specified boxes, all of them remain empty exactly when every throw avoids that set.}
\textnormal{The quantity just defined is the sum of the probabilities over all sets of that size. The logarithmic expansion and the given number of throws give its limit.}
\textnormal{These are the finite Bonferroni bounds. First take the number of boxes to infinity with the truncation fixed; only then let the truncation grow.}
statement: \begin{gathered}\textnormal{Throw balls independently}\\\textnormal{and uniformly into n boxes.}\\\textnormal{The number of throws is}\\r_n=\lfloor n\ln n+n\ln 2\rfloor\\p_n=\Pr(\textnormal{every box is occupied})\\\lim_{n\to\infty}p_n\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: For n boxes and r_n=floor(n log n+n log m) independent uniform throws, any specified j boxes are all empty with probability(1-j/n)^r_n.

For each fixed nonnegative j, C(n,j)(1-j/n)^r_n tends to m^-j/j!: expand log(1-j/n)=-j/n+O(n^-2), and use C(n,j)~n^j/j!. The floor changes the exponent by less than one and hence changes the factor by a ratio tending to one.
Bonferroni inequalities bound the no-empty-box probability between its finite inclusion-exclusion truncations of odd and even orders. First send n to infinity with truncation order fixed.
Then send the truncation order to infinity. Both limiting truncations converge to sum(-1)^j/(m^j j!)=exp(-1/m). No exchange with an n-dependent infinite alternating sum has been assumed.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{After dividing both coordinates by the prescribed greatest common divisor, count coprime pairs.}
\textnormal{Let the Möbius function be zero for integers with a repeated prime factor, and otherwise the sign determined by the number of distinct prime factors.}
\mu(d)=(-1)^k\quad\textnormal{when }d\textnormal{ is a product of }k\textnormal{ distinct primes},\qquad\mu(1)=1
\textnormal{The divisor identity follows by choosing subsets of the distinct prime factors: for a nonunit integer the signs sum to a positive power of zero.}
\textnormal{The right-hand side is summable, so dominated convergence for series passes the limit through the divisor sum.}
\textnormal{Absolute convergence permits expansion of the Euler products into prime factorizations. The two reciprocal Euler products cancel.}

analyticCertificate: Dividing both coordinates by m reduces gcd(a,b)=m to a coprime pair inside the square of side floor(N/m).
The divisor identity sum_(d|g)mu(d)=1 for g=1 and0 otherwise turns the exact count into sum_(d<=N/m)mu(d)floor(N/(md))^2.
After division by N^2, each d term tends to mu(d)/(m^2d^2), and its absolute value is at most1/(m^2d^2). The summable majorant justifies passage through the series.
Absolute convergence and unique prime factorization give sum mu(d)/d^2=product_p(1-p^-2)=1/zeta(2)=6/pi^2. Thus the density is6/(pi^2m^2).

solutionSteps: \textnormal{In the determinant expansion by column multilinearity, the quadratic coefficient selects two diagonal increments. Each selection leaves the principal minor obtained by deleting those two coordinates.}
\textnormal{A tridiagonal path block of length }k\textnormal{ with diagonal entries two and neighbor entries minus one has determinant }D_k\textnormal{.}
\textnormal{Deleting two cycle vertices at cyclic distance }r\textnormal{ leaves path lengths }r-1\textnormal{ and }5-r-1\textnormal{. Their determinant product is }r(5-r)\textnormal{.}
\textnormal{Each unordered pair was counted twice by starting vertex and cyclic distance. Finally convert the quadratic coefficient to a second derivative.}

analyticCertificate: Multilinearity in columns selects either the old column or x times its coordinate vector. Selecting two coordinate columns leaves the corresponding principal minor with positive sign; thus the x squared coefficient is their sum. Every unordered vertex pair is counted twice by the n starting vertices and distances 1,...,n-1, including antipodal pairs. Removing the pair splits the cycle into two path blocks, with an empty block assigned determinant one. Their exact recurrence gives product r(n-r), and summing r and r squared yields the displayed formula.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For nonzero inputs, repeated differentiation has a leading oscillatory term whose power drops by two at each step.}
\textnormal{Here }\phi_k\textnormal{ is sine or cosine, and }\varepsilon_k\in\{-1,1\}\textnormal{. The chain rule cycles the leading trigonometric factor and its sign.}
\textnormal{Induction therefore gives all these derivatives at zero, each equal to zero. Through the preceding order, the punctured derivatives also tend to zero and are continuous.}

\textnormal{Reciprocal-phase sequences make the leading term approach opposite nonzero values. This derivative is discontinuous, and dividing it by the input also prevents the next derivative at zero from existing.}
statement: \begin{gathered}f(x)=\begin{cases}x^{10}\sin(1/x),&x\ne0,\\0,&x=0.\end{cases}\\\textnormal{Find (r,s), where r is the}\\\textnormal{greatest integer for which f}\\\textnormal{has an rth derivative at 0,}\\\textnormal{and s is the greatest integer}\\\textnormal{for which all derivatives}\\\textnormal{through order s are continuous}\\\textnormal{on a neighborhood of 0.}\end{gathered}

analyticCertificate: Write each punctured derivative as A_k(x)sin(1/x)+B_k(x)cos(1/x). The recurrence A_(k+1)=A_k prime+B_k/x squared, B_(k+1)=B_k prime-A_k/x squared shows its smallest power is 2m+2-2k, with coefficient vector cycling (1,0),(0,-1),(-1,0),(0,1). All other terms have at least one higher power. For k<=m+1, the preceding derivative divided by x is O(|x|^(2m+3-2k)), which tends to zero, proving the derivative at zero inductively. For k<=m, the punctured derivative tends to zero, proving continuity. At k=m+1, choose positive sequences whose reciprocal phase makes the leading sine/cosine equal 1 and -1; the O(x) remainder vanishes. Hence this derivative is discontinuous. Along a sequence with leading value 1, its difference quotient at zero is unbounded, so derivative m+2 does not exist.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Expand the Newton map about its fixed point, using a small displacement from that point.}
\textnormal{Composing the map squares the previous leading error and multiplies its coefficient by the same quadratic coefficient.}
\textnormal{The eighth derivative is the eighth Taylor coefficient multiplied by the factorial of its order.}

analyticCertificate: The rational Newton map is analytic near 1 and has vanishing first derivative but nonzero quadratic coefficient c. If E(z)=a z^r+O(z^(r+1)), then N(1+E)-1=c a squared z^(2r)+O(z^(2r+1)). Applying this twice to the first error gives orders 2,4,8 and coefficients c,c cubed,c to the seventh power. No lower-order Taylor term survives, and the eighth derivative is 8 factorial times that coefficient. The independent exact truncated-jet composition checks this finite claim without assuming the final formula.
